item.title: ComfyUI-KJNodes Introduces Enhanced Set/Get Node Functionality
item.description:
ComfyUI-KJNodes Introduces Enhanced Set/Get Node Functionality

🔍 Overview

The ComfyUI-KJNodes project has recently undergone a significant update, introducing enhanced functionalities for Set/Get nodes within the ComfyUI framework. This update focuses on extending support to both legacy and nodes 2.0, alongside promoting cross-subgraph interconnectivity.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Backward Compatibility: The rewrite maintains compatibility with earlier versions, ensuring seamless integration with existing workflows.
  • Subgraph Functionality: Set/Get nodes now operate across parent and child subgraphs, facilitating broader interactions within multi-tiered structures.
  • New Operations:
    • Convert link to Set/Get using a right-click on any link midpoint.
    • Batch convert selected node outputs to Set/Get pairs.
    • The canvas right-click menu supports the conversion of outputs on selected nodes.
  • Key Shortcuts:
    • Ctrl+Shift+S: Add Set nodes.
    • Ctrl+Shift+G: Add Get nodes.
    • Ctrl+Shift+L: Toggle visibility of all connections.
  • Settings Enhancements: New settings for managing link visibility, keyboard shortcuts without conflicting with other actions, and sprite appearance based on connections.
  • Conversion Features: Right-clicking a SetNode adds a corresponding GetNode, and double-clicking a GetNode navigates to its paired SetNode.
  • Type and Color Update: Nodes now reflect type changes when inputs or outputs are disconnected, ensuring consistency in visual feedback.
  • Settings Structure: Settings have been reorganized under KJNodes > Set & Get and KJNodes > General categories for improved navigation.

💡 Why It Matters

This update enhances user interaction and workflow efficiency within the ComfyUI ecosystem. The integration of Set/Get functionalities across subgraphs and the addition of user-friendly features signifies an advancement in customization capabilities, empowering users to build more complex and interconnected AI pipelines.

🚀 Availability

To begin using these features, users should:

  1. Clone the custom_nodes repo to the custom_nodes folder.
  2. Install dependencies using pip install -r requirements.txt.

For portable installs, utilize:

1

custom_setup/ComfyUI_windows_portable-folder/python_embeded/python.exe -m pip install -r ComfyUI/custom_nodes/ComfyUI-KJNodes/requirements.txt

#ComfyUI #AIToolkit #KJNodes #SetGetNodes #Subgraphs #NodeOptimization

Source: kijai/ComfyUI-KJNodes

item.title: PSF Expands Security Team and Adds New AI Development Entries
item.description:
PSF Expands Security Team and Adds New AI Development Entries

The Python Software Foundation (PSF) has expanded its Developers in Residence program to include three security developers, while recent entries in AI development include running Datasette in the browser and utilizing local large language models.

👥 Security Team Expansion

The PSF operates the Developers in Residence program, which now includes three security developers. One of the new members is Brett Smith. These developers are focused on helping secure Python, PyPI, and the wider ecosystem. The PSF also employs a small staff team to keep operations running, which includes running PyCon US annually and sponsoring core developer sprints.

🧩 Recent AI Development Entries

Recent technical entries document various AI and Python-based developments:

  • Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser using service workers and Pyodide, noted on 17th November 2026.
  • Locating the source of a mysterious beep using Claude, noted on 9th November 2026.
  • Hiding slop PR descriptions behind HTML details tags, noted on 9th November 2026.
  • Running Qwen 3.8 27B on a laptop to interpret model weights, noted on 3rd November 2026.

#Python #AI #Security #Datasette #Pyodide

Source: The PSF end-of-year fundraiser

item.title: NVIDIA Introduces cuDLA Python Bindings for Deep Learning Accelerator Workflows
item.description:
NVIDIA Introduces cuDLA Python Bindings for Deep Learning Accelerator Workflows

NVIDIA has introduced the cuda.bindings.cudla module in cuda-bindings 13.3.0 as part of the CUDA Python project. This thin, Cython-generated Python layer exposes the cuDLA C++ API directly to Python, allowing developers to manage NVIDIA Deep Learning Accelerator (DLA) execution without writing C++ runtime code.

🔍 Overview

NVIDIA DLA platforms provide dedicated fixed-function hardware for deep learning inference. On platforms like the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, DLA executes supported neural network operations to offload inference work from the GPU, improving power efficiency and freeing GPU capacity for other application tasks. While DLA does not support as many layers as a GPU, it supports a wide variety of layers used in popular neural network architectures.

🧩 Architecture and API Capabilities

The cuda.bindings.cudla module exposes the runtime API needed for hybrid-mode workflows:

  • API Components: Contains thirteen functions, nine data types, and eight enums for hybrid-mode management.
  • Hybrid Mode Execution: Setting cudla.Mode.CUDA_DLA enables hybrid mode, where DLA tasks are submitted through CUDA streams.
  • Unified Pipelines: CUDA streams coordinate GPU and DLA work so that preprocessing kernels, DLA inference, and postprocessing kernels can be enqueued and executed in order on the same stream.
  • Platform Consistency: The API is identical on Jetson Orin and NVIDIA RTX Spark Windows AI laptops, extending cuDLA execution to mainstream developer laptops.

⚙️ Compilation and Runtime Details

Running DLA workloads requires specific setup and compilation parameters depending on the workflow phase:

Process Step Details Requirements & Behavior
Model Compilation TensorRT trtexec tool compiles a trained model into a DLA loadable Requires TensorRT (example targets TensorRT 11.4.1 with CUDA 13.4 Update 1)
Standalone Mode buildDLAStandalone produces a raw DLA loadable Does not require TensorRT at inference time
Core Selection useDLACore=0 Targets the first DLA engine on Orin
Precision Setting Precision is derived from model tensor types in TensorRT 11 --fp16 and --int8 flags are no longer supported
Model Preprocessing Trimming ONNX graph head and tail layers Necessary when network layers are DLA-incompatible
Layout Selection I/O format options Selects CHW16 layout

🚀 Environment Requirements

  • Runtime Dependencies: To run an existing DLA loadable, only libcudla.so is required. On Jetson Orin, NVIDIA JetPack supplies libcudla.so automatically without requiring a separate cuDLA SDK or extra runtime libraries.
  • Python Version: Python 3.10 is the minimum required version. JetPack’s default Python version may be older than 3.10.

#NVIDIA #CUDA #Python #Jetson #DeepLearning

Source: Run Native DLA Inference in Python on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin Using cuDLA | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA KvikIO Python Library Demonstrates Direct GPU Storage Access via GPUDirect Storage
item.description:
NVIDIA KvikIO Python Library Demonstrates Direct GPU Storage Access via GPUDirect Storage

NVIDIA’s Magnum IO GPUDirect Storage (GDS) now works with the KvikIO Python library to let AI applications move data directly from storage into GPU memory, bypassing the CPU.

🔍 Overview

  • GPU applications are processing ever‑growing datasets with increasingly powerful accelerators.
  • The 2025 Stanford AI Index reports that compute for notable AI models has been doubling roughly every five months, while the size of datasets used to train LLMs has been doubling roughly every eight months.
  • As computation and data scale together, moving data efficiently from storage becomes a necessity for keeping accelerators supplied.
  • NVIDIA Magnum IO GPUDirect Storage (GDS) addresses this challenge by enabling a direct data path between supported storage and GPU memory.
  • The direct path avoids unnecessary staging through CPU memory and reduces overall CPU utilization in the system.
  • GDS is supported by a growing ecosystem that includes many major storage vendors.
  • At the application layer, Python plays a central role in modern AI development; as of August 2025, nearly half of all new AI projects on GitHub were built primarily in Python.

🧩 How It Works

Component Role
GPUDirect Storage (GDS) Enables a direct data path between supported storage and GPU memory.
cuFile C library and API through which applications and frameworks access GDS.
KvikIO Python and C++ library that sits above cuFile, providing high‑level, idiomatic interfaces and additional controls over how I/O requests are performed.
  • The application supplies a file‑system path and a GPU buffer.
  • KvikIO decides whether to route the request through cuFile (direct path) or use its POSIX compatibility path, which stages data through host memory.
  • When cuFile is selected, KvikIO registers the file and issues the I/O using the target GPU buffer.
  • cuFile then determines the actual transfer path based on system support, the file system, and its configuration; it may use the accelerated GDS path or fall back to a CPU‑staged compatibility path.
  • Reaching the cuFile API confirms that KvikIO selected cuFile, but does not by itself confirm that the accelerated GDS path was activated.

⚙️ Tutorial Highlights

  • Demonstrates how to use the NVIDIA KvikIO Python API to configure storage I/O, read data into GPU memory, and confirm that the accelerated path within GDS was activated.
  • Shows how to inspect KvikIO and cuFile settings that influence the path each operation takes.
  • Tested on an x86_64 system with an NVIDIA H100 GPU, CUDA 13.3, and cuFile 1.18.
  • The system used a local NVMe device formatted with ext4; a PIX connection between the GPU and NVMe device means the path traverses at most one PCIe bridge.
  • IOMMU and ACS were disabled to preserve PCIe peer‑to‑peer transfers, and the nvidia-fs kernel module was loaded to provide the accelerated path.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Doubling compute and dataset sizes increase pressure on the storage‑to‑GPU data pipeline.
  • Direct storage‑to‑GPU transfers reduce CPU overhead, freeing CPU resources for other parts of the AI workload.
  • Providing a high‑level Python interface (KvikIO) aligns with the fact that nearly half of new AI projects are Python‑centric, lowering the barrier for developers to adopt accelerated I/O.
  • A growing storage‑vendor ecosystem around GDS broadens hardware compatibility for future AI systems.

#NVIDIA #GPUDirectStorage #KvikIO #AI #Python

Source: How to Read Data into GPU Memory in Python with NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage | NVIDIA Technical Blog
